questions.prompt: For steepest descent with exact line search on \(f(x) = \tfrac12 x^T A x + b^T x\), with \(A\) positive definite and \(\kappa = \lambda_{\max}(A)/\lambda_{\min}(A)\), the excess \(f - f^\star\) contracts by at most
questions.explanation: The classical bound multiplies the excess by \(((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1))^2\). The unsquared factor bounds the error in the \(A\)-norm, and the excess is half the square of that norm, so the excess carries the square. Using \(\kappa\) itself is larger than 1 for \(\kappa > 1\) and cannot be a contraction. The factor \(1/\kappa^2\) is a different estimate and is not this bound.

questions.prompt: The Hessian eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(3\), so \(\kappa = 3\). What is the contraction factor \(((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1))^2\)?
questions.explanation: The ratio is \((3 - 1)/(3 + 1) = 1/2\), and the factor on the excess is the square, \(1/4\). Reporting \(1/2\) stops before the square. Reporting \(3\) is the condition number. Reporting \(2\) is \(\kappa - 1\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.

questions.explanation: At \(\kappa = 1\) the factor is \(0\), which matches one-step termination on a multiple of the identity. As \(\kappa\) grows, \((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)\) grows toward \(1\), and so does its square. A larger factor is a slower guarantee. The factor is not equal to \(\kappa\), and both \(\kappa - 1\) and \(\kappa + 1\) are positive for \(\kappa > 1\), so the factor stays positive.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.
options: increases toward \(1\), so the guaranteed linear rate gets slower
decreases toward \(0\), so the guarantee gets faster

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that turns eigenvalues into a bound on the next excess. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The eigenvalues are the inputs. Their ratio is \(\kappa\), and the contraction factor is built from that ratio by subtracting, adding, dividing, and squaring. Only then is the factor applied to the excess. Squaring before the condition number exists has nothing to square. Multiplying the excess by an eigenvalue, rather than by the factor, is a different quantity.

questions.figure_alt: A two-by-two array with labels on the diagonal.
steps: Read off the largest and smallest eigenvalues of the positive definite Hessian.
Form the condition number \(\kappa\) as their ratio.
Multiply the current excess by that square to bound the excess at the next exact steepest step.

questions.prompt: The contraction factor on the excess is at most \(1/4\). Which of these Hessian eigenvalue pairs qualify?
questions.explanation:
The factor \(((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1))^2\) is at most \(1/4\) exactly when \(\kappa \le 3\).
• Eigenvalues \(1, 2\) give \(\kappa = 2\).
• Eigenvalues \(2, 6\) give \(\kappa = 3\), and the factor equals \(1/4\).
• Eigenvalues \(4, 4\) give \(\kappa = 1\), and the factor is \(0\).
• Eigenvalues \(1, 9\) give \(\kappa = 9\), and the factor is \(0.64\).
• Eigenvalues \(1, 7\) give \(\kappa = 7\), and the factor is \(0.5625\).

questions.prompt: The current excess is \(\mathrm{gap} > 0\) and the condition number is \(r > 1\). The bound on the next excess equals
questions.explanation: Multiply the excess by the squared factor. Both names appear. Dropping the square leaves the \(A\)-norm factor, which is the wrong power for the excess. Using \((r + 1)/(r - 1)\) inverts the factor and produces a number larger than 1. Subtracting the factor from the excess, instead of multiplying, is a different operation.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.

questions.prompt: A note treats \(\kappa = 3\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The ratio of eigenvalues is \(3\), and \((3 - 1)/(3 + 1) = 1/2\). The excess is quadratic in the \(A\)-norm error, so the factor on the excess is the square, \(1/4\). The false step stops at \(1/2\). The last step is the right monotonicity: a larger condition number pushes the factor toward 1.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
steps: The contraction factor for the excess \(f - f^\star\) is \(1/2\).
Increasing \(\kappa\) moves the factor toward \(1\), which is a slower guarantee.
reasons: The excess picks up the square, so the factor is \(1/4\), not \(1/2\).
A larger condition number makes the factor smaller.

questions.prompt: The condition number is \(5\), and the current excess is \(9\). What is the bound on the next excess?
questions.explanation: The unsquared quotient is \((5 - 1)/(5 + 1) = 2/3\). Its square is \(4/9\). Then \(9 \cdot (4/9) = 4\). Reporting \(6\) uses \(2/3\) without the square, since \(9 \cdot 2/3 = 6\). Reporting \(5\) is the condition number. Reporting \(9\) leaves the excess unchanged.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.

questions.prompt: When the factor \(((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1))^2\) lies in \((0, 1)\), the bound is a statement of
questions.explanation: Multiplying the excess by the same number in \((0, 1)\) at every step is linear convergence. Quadratic convergence would square the error. A factor in \((0, 1)\) still goes to zero, so it is not a failure. Finite termination for every condition number is false. It happens for the factor \(0\), which is the case \(\kappa = 1\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.
options: finite termination in two steps for every \(\kappa\)

questions.prompt: Conjugate gradients improve the dependence on this condition number by
questions.explanation: The steepest-descent factor approaches \(1\) like \(1 - 2/\kappa\). Conjugate gradients use an inner product built from the Hessian and have a contraction that behaves like \(((\sqrt{\kappa} - 1)/(\sqrt{\kappa} + 1))^2\), which is much closer to zero for large \(\kappa\). Squaring \(\kappa\) inside the steepest factor would make the bound worse. The step length is not \(\kappa\). The Hessian is exactly what the conjugacy uses.

replacing \(\kappa\) by \(\kappa^2\) in the same steepest-descent factor
using a step length equal to \(\kappa\)

questions.prompt: The Hessian eigenvalues are \(2\) and \(8\). What is the contraction factor on the excess?
questions.explanation: The condition number is \(8/2 = 4\). Then \((4 - 1)/(4 + 1) = 3/5\), and the square is \(9/25 = 0.36\). Reporting \(0.6\) stops before the square. Reporting \(4\) is the condition number. Reporting \(0.25\) is the factor for \(\kappa = 3\), not for \(\kappa = 4\).

questions.prompt: A momentum step such as the heavy-ball update uses this condition number to
questions.explanation: The heavy-ball iteration adds a multiple of the previous step. On a quadratic, that weight can be chosen from \(\kappa\), and the resulting rate beats \(((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1))^2\). The objective is not set equal to \(\kappa\). The eigenvalues stay whatever the Hessian has. The gradient is still evaluated.
